analysis.one_liner: Repeals tax breaks, royalty discounts, liability caps, and federal financing for fossil fuel production.
analysis.headline: Referred to nine House committees in November 2013, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would end a long list of federal supports for coal, oil, and natural gas companies: it would stop the Interior Department from cutting royalty payments on offshore leases, raise the standard royalty rate on federal coal, oil, and gas leases from 12.5% to 18.75%, remove the legal cap on what companies must pay for oil spills, and shut down Department of Energy fossil fuel research and federal loan and grant programs that support fossil fuel projects here and abroad. On the tax side, it would terminate more than a dozen preferences — including enhanced oil recovery credits, percentage depletion for coal, the domestic manufacturing deduction for oil and gas, and the last-in, first-out accounting method for fuel companies — and impose a 13% tax on oil and gas taken from the Gulf of Mexico's federal waters. It would also require reports to identify and eliminate any remaining fossil fuel subsidies in the tax code.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently fund tens of billions of dollars in federal fossil fuel subsidies (the bill's findings cite over $72 billion from 2002 through 2008, versus $12.2 billion for renewables); coastal communities, who would gain stronger recourse against companies responsible for oil spills; and the federal Treasury, which would collect higher royalties and a new 13% Gulf of Mexico production tax.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Interior Secretary's authority to reduce or eliminate royalty payments on offshore oil and gas leases, and repeals shallow-water and deep-water royalty relief from the Energy Policy Act of 2005 [S2].
Raises the minimum federal royalty rate on coal, oil, and natural gas leases from 12.5% to 18.75%, meaning the public gets a larger share of the value of resources taken from federal land [S2][S3].

Removes the $75 million cap and other liability limits on offshore facilities and pipeline operators for oil spill damages, including a special provision for pipelines carrying tar-sands-type diluted bitumen [S2][S3].

Terminates the Department of Energy's Office of Fossil Energy Research and Development, blocks DOT funding for rail or port projects transporting fossil fuel, prohibits Rural Electrification Act loans for fossil fuel projects, and rescinds and bars future funding for World Bank, Export-Import Bank, and OPIC financing of fossil fuel projects [S2][S3].

Terminates more than a dozen tax preferences for fossil fuel companies, including the enhanced oil recovery credit, marginal well credits, percentage depletion for coal, the domestic manufacturing deduction for oil and gas, intangible drilling cost deductions, and LIFO accounting for oil, gas, and coal companies, while imposing a 13% severance tax on Gulf of Mexico outer continental shelf production [S3].

Directs the Treasury Secretary to report within a year on every remaining federal law providing a fossil fuel production subsidy and to eliminate accelerated depreciation for any fossil fuel property receiving one [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal, oil, and natural gas companies, which would lose tax preferences worth billions, pay higher royalties on federal leases, face unlimited oil spill liability, and lose access to federal research, loan, and export financing; some of these costs could be passed through to consumers in energy prices.

drawbacks.text: The new 13% tax on Gulf of Mexico oil and gas, the higher royalty rate, and the increased Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund fee (rising from 8 to 10 cents per barrel) would raise production costs that producers could pass through to consumers in fuel prices [S2][S3].

The bill reaches beyond oil and gas: it repeals the domestic manufacturing deduction for hard mineral mining generally and ends capital gains treatment for coal royalties, raising costs for mining operations beyond the fuel sector [S3].

Eliminating federal fossil energy research and loan guarantees could slow development of technologies such as carbon capture that some see as necessary for managing emissions from fuels that will be burned regardless.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill — ending subsidies to highly profitable fossil fuel companies and making spillers fully liable for damages — transfers costs from taxpayers to the companies that profit from public resources, and the bill's own findings note the five largest oil corporations earned over $1 trillion in profits in the prior decade. The main honest cost is that some added taxes and fees could show up at the pump, and the bill's breadth (reaching into hard mineral mining and rail and port financing) would have required significant administrative sorting.

outcome.mechanism: After being referred to nine House committees on the day it was introduced, the bill received no hearings, no markup, and no floor vote, and it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Keith Ellison introduced the bill on November 21, 2013, with 12 Democratic cosponsors including Reps. Conyers, Grijalva, Blumenauer, Honda, Huffman, Nolan, Serrano, Lee, Grayson, and Cohen [S3][S4].

The House referred it to nine standing committees — Ways and Means, Transportation and Infrastructure, Natural Resources, Science, Space, and Technology, Energy and Commerce, Agriculture, Appropriations, Financial Services, and Foreign Affairs — with portions later sent to six subcommittees [S5].
No committee reported the bill, no vote was ever scheduled, and the final recorded action in the bill's history is a subcommittee referral from December 2013 [S5].

The bill's findings acknowledge the political context: the oil and gas industry spent $105 million on lobbying in the first three quarters of 2013, which the findings describe as effective at protecting the industry's tax loopholes and subsidies [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal, oil, and natural gas companies, which kept their tax preferences, 12.5% royalty rates, liability caps, and access to federal research and export financing because the bill never reached a vote.

sides.party_line_note: All 13 members who sponsored or cosponsored the bill were Democrats; no Republican signed on, the bill was referred to committees run by a Republican majority, and it never reached a vote.

industries.note: The bill terminates roughly a dozen tax preferences (enhanced oil recovery credits, intangible drilling costs, the domestic manufacturing deduction, LIFO accounting), raises the federal royalty rate to 18.75%, and imposes a 13% Gulf of Mexico severance tax. These companies are among the most profitable in the country, and their cost savings come from federal tax and royalty treatment paid for by taxpayers.

The bill raises coal lease royalties from 12.5% to 18.75%, repeals percentage depletion and capital gains treatment for coal, and orders a study of whether Powder River Basin coal is leased below fair market value. Public land coal has long been sold at rates that independent analyses have called below-market.

The bill removes the cap on their liability for oil spills and denies them a tax deduction for spill damages, shifting catastrophic spill costs back onto the companies responsible rather than the Oil Spill Liability Trust Fund, which is financed by a per-barrel fee and ultimately by taxpayers.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel export and development financiers (Export-Import Bank, OPIC, World Bank-funded projects)
industries.note: The bill rescinds unobligated funds and bars future use of U.S. money at these institutions for any project supporting fossil fuel production, ending a channel through which U.S. taxpayers back overseas coal, oil, and gas projects.
The bill repeals the domestic manufacturing deduction for hard mineral mining generally, a tax benefit that extends beyond fuel producers.
